title: Inventory and Stock Types
readerIntent: Understand the inventory states and policies needed for checkout, fulfillment, and enterprise operations.
summary: Inventory separates on-hand stock, available-to-sell, reservations, allocations, pre-order, backorder, overbooking, serialized stock, movements, and reconciliation so checkout can make safe commitments.

sections.heading: Inventory is more than a number
paragraphs: A product page often shows a simple message such as `In stock`. Internally, that result may depend on warehouse balances, stock pools, reserved quantities, damaged stock, safety stock, unit conversion, sourcing zones, backorder policy, pre-order limits, external WMS evidence, and checkout commitments.

Nodics treats Inventory as the authority for these decisions. Product identifies the item. Cart and Order request commitments. Inventory calculates and records whether the business can safely promise the quantity.

sections.heading: Core stock concepts
items: On-hand stock: recorded physical or logical quantity currently held by the business.
Available-to-sell: quantity that can be offered after reservations, safety rules, and policy deductions.
Reserved stock: quantity temporarily held for cart, order, or process demand before fulfillment allocation.
Allocated stock: quantity assigned to a specific order, warehouse, or fulfillment path.
Issued stock: quantity removed from inventory through shipment, pickup, consumption, adjustment, or another movement.
Returned stock: quantity coming back through return handling, inspection, restock, quarantine, or disposal.
Safety stock: protected quantity that should not be sold except by policy override.
Damaged or quarantined stock: quantity that exists physically but should not be promised to customers.

sections.heading: Pre-order, backorder, and overbooking
items: Pre-order means the business intentionally sells before stock is physically available, usually against a planned future supply date or launch capacity.
Backorder means the customer order is accepted when current stock is insufficient, with fulfillment expected after replenishment.
Allowed overbooking means the business intentionally accepts demand above the configured pre-order or stock capacity. It must be explicit policy, not accidental negative stock.

For example, a product may have pre-order capacity `100` and allowed overbooking `20`. Checkout may accept up to `120`, but the overbooked quantity can require advance payment, extra approval, different promise messaging, or stricter cancellation rules.

Overbooking should always record policy evidence: original capacity, current committed quantity, overbooking allowance, accepted overbooked quantity, required advance amount, user/system actor, and effective time.

sections.heading: Serialized and quantity-level inventory
paragraphs: Some products are not just anonymous quantities. Electronics, vehicles, luxury goods, regulated items, warranties, repairable goods, and rentals may require serial numbers or asset identities. In that case, quantity `3` may become three individual stock units, each with its own serial number, condition, warranty, or provider evidence.
Nodics should keep the normal quantity model for most commerce flows and allow customer modules to extend allocation evidence with serialized inventory references when the business requires it.
items: Use quantity-level reservation and allocation for standard stock.
Use serialized evidence when one physical unit must be tracked independently.
Do not put serial-number business logic into Product or Axis. Inventory remains the authority.

sections.heading: External inventory providers
paragraphs: Many enterprises use warehouse management systems, point-of-sale systems, ERPs, marketplace inventory feeds, or third-party logistics partners. Nodics must integrate with those systems through provider adapters and reconciliation, not by exposing internal stock tables directly.

External providers can report availability, accept reservations, confirm allocations, provide shipment evidence, or send movement updates. Nodics records the provider evidence and applies authoritative Inventory changes through governed operations.

sections.heading: Inventory decisions during checkout
items: Is the requested product and unit eligible for sale in the current store/site/country/channel?
Which warehouses, pools, or providers can source the requested quantity?
How much is on-hand, reserved, available-to-sell, pre-orderable, backorderable, or overbookable?
Can the requested quantity be split across warehouses or delivery groups?
Should the system reserve immediately, reserve after payment authorization, or defer reservation until order approval?
If stock changes while checkout is in progress, should checkout fail, retry, recalculate, or accept according to policy?

sections.heading: Customization guidance
items: Add new inventory policy through customer module configuration and services, not by changing Product or Cart.
Add external WMS, POS, ERP, or marketplace integration through provider adapters with idempotency and reconciliation.
Add serialized inventory by extending Inventory schemas and allocation evidence while preserving the same Cart and Order contracts.
Expose new Axis fields through backend presentation metadata and reusable schema detail/list components.
